source_text: Videamus nunc, si et apostolus formam vocabuli istius secundum Genesim observat, sexui deputans illud, sic mulierem vocans virginem Mariam quemadmodum et Genesis Evam. Scribens enim ad Galatas, Misit, inquit, deus filium suum factum ex muliere, quam utique virginem constat fuisse, licet Hebion resistat. Agnosco et angelum Gabrielem ad virginem missum. Sed cum benedicit illam, inter mulieres, non inter virgines deputat: Benedicta tu inter mulieres. Sciebat et angelus mulierem etiam virginem dici. Sed et ad haec duo ingeniose quidam respondisse sibi visus est, quoniam quidem desponsata est Maria, idcirco et ab angelo et ab apostolo mulierem pronuntiatam. Desponsata enim quodammodo nupta. Tamen inter quodammodo et verum satis interest, duntaxat hoc in loco. Nam alibi ita sane habendum est. Nunc vero, non quasi iam nuptam mulierem Mariam pronuntiaverunt, sed quasi nihilominus feminam, etiamsi non sponsam, quasi hoc a primordio dictam. Illud enim praeiudicet necesse est a quo forma descendit. Ceterum quod pertineat ad hoc capitulum, si hic desponsatae adaequatur, ut ideo mulier dicta sit Maria, non qua femina, sed qua maritata, iam ergo Christus non ex virgine natus est, quia ex desponsata, quae virgo esse desierit hoc nomine. Quod si ex virgine natus est, licet et desponsata, tamen integra, agnosce mulierem etiam virginem, etiam integram dici. Hic certe nibil prophetice dictum videri postest, ut futuram mulierem, id est nuptam, apostolus nominarit, dicendo factum ex muliere. Non enim poterat posteriorem mulierem nominare, de qua Christus nasci non habebat, id est virum passam, sed illa, quae erat praesens, quae erat virgo et mulier vocabatur post vocabuli huius proprietatem, secundum primordii formam virgini et ita universo mulierum generi defensam.
thought_title: Paul and Gabriel call Mary 'woman' while she is still a virgin
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that the word 'woman' in Scripture includes virgins, and now turns to the apostle Paul and the angel Gabriel as witnesses.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see now, if also the apostle observes the form of this word according to Genesis, assigning it to the sex, thus calling the virgin Mary 'woman' just as Genesis also called Eve 'woman'. For writing to the Galatians, he says, 'God sent his Son made from a woman,' whom it is certainly agreed was a virgin, although Hebion resists. I recognize also the angel Gabriel sent to the virgin. But when he blesses her, he counts her among women, not among virgins: 'Blessed are you among women.' The angel also knew that a virgin is called 'woman.' But also to these two points someone has thought he answered cleverly, because indeed Mary was betrothed, and for that reason she was called 'woman' both by the angel and by the apostle. For a betrothed woman is in some way married. Yet between 'in some way' and 'truly' there is enough difference, at least in this place. For elsewhere it must indeed be taken so. But now, they did not call Mary 'woman' as if already married, but as nonetheless female, even if not a bride, as if this was said from the beginning. For that must prejudge from which the form descends. But as far as pertains to this chapter, if here she is made equal to a betrothed woman, so that Mary was called 'woman' not as female but as married, then already Christ was not born from a virgin, because he was born from a betrothed woman, who would have ceased to be a virgin by this name. But if he was born from a virgin, although also betrothed, yet intact, recognize that a woman is called also a virgin, also intact. Here certainly nothing can seem to have been said prophetically, as if the apostle named a future woman, that is a married woman, by saying 'made from a woman.' For he could not name a later woman, from whom Christ was not going to be born, that is one who had suffered a man, but that woman who was present, who was a virgin and was called 'woman' according to the proper meaning of this word, according to the form of the beginning defended for the virgin and so for the whole race of women.

choices.why: Keeps 'form' as the pattern or model of usage established in Genesis, matching Tertullian's argument that the word's usage descends from the beginning.
Renders deputo as assigning/reckoning to the female sex, preserving the idea that 'woman' is a term of sex, not marital status.
Literal rendering of the Pauline phrase, keeping 'made' for factum and 'from' for ex, as the source of Christ's human birth.
Preserves the concessive force of quodammodo, which Tertullian immediately contrasts with 'truly' (verum).

choices.why: Literal rendering of the euphemism for sexual intercourse, keeping the passive force of patior and the bluntness of Tertullian's expression.

choices.why: Renders proprietas as 'proper meaning,' the word's own intrinsic sense, which Tertullian says belongs to the female sex from the beginning.

pass_b_english: Let us now see whether the apostle also follows the pattern of this word according to Genesis, assigning it to the female sex, calling the virgin Mary a woman just as Genesis calls Eve one. Writing to the Galatians, he says, “God sent his Son, made from a woman” (Galatians 4:4). And she was certainly a virgin, even if the heretic Hebion resists that claim.

I recognize too that the angel Gabriel was sent to a virgin. But when he blesses her, he reckons her among women, not among virgins: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28). The angel also knew that even a virgin is called a woman.

But someone has thought he answered these two points cleverly: since Mary was betrothed, she was therefore pronounced a woman by both the angel and the apostle. For a betrothed woman is in some way married. Yet there is a great difference between “in some way” and “truly,” at least in this place. Elsewhere it may be taken so. But here they did not pronounce Mary a woman as if she were already married, but as nonetheless female, even if not a bride, as one called this from the beginning. For that original pattern must determine the matter from which the form descends.

As for this point, if a betrothed woman is made equal to a married one, so that Mary was called a woman not because she was female but because she was married, then Christ was not born of a virgin, because he was born of a betrothed woman who had ceased to be a virgin by this name. But if he was born of a virgin, though also betrothed, yet untouched, then recognize that even a virgin, even an untouched one, is called a woman.

Here certainly nothing can seem to have been said prophetically, as if the apostle named her a future woman, that is, a married one, by saying “made from a woman.” For he could not name a later woman from whom Christ was not to be born, that is, one who had known a man. He named the one who was present, who was a virgin and was called a woman according to the proper meaning of this word, according to the pattern of the beginning, and so this meaning is defended for the virgin and for the whole race of women.

last_rejected.why: Latin means a woman who has taken a man (i.e., married), not one who has suffered a man.
last_rejected.ruling: patior can mean 'to suffer/undergo'; 'suffered a man' = had sexual relations, a valid rendering of virum passam

last_rejected.quote: For that original pattern must determine the matter from which the form descends.
last_rejected.source_quote: Illud enim praeiudicet necesse est a quo forma descendit.
last_rejected.why: The source of the pattern must settle the question. English reverses subject and object.
last_rejected.fix: For that from which the pattern descends must necessarily settle the question.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Illud ... a quo forma descendit' is the origin, which must settle the matter. The English has the pattern as subject, so the sense holds, though 'the matter' is clumsy.

last_rejected.quote: if a betrothed woman is made equal to a married one
last_rejected.why: Mary is classed with a betrothed woman. English equates betrothed with married.
last_rejected.fix: if she is here classed with a betrothed woman, so that Mary was called a woman not as female but as married
last_rejected.ruling: The argument rests on 'Desponsata enim quodammodo nupta': betrothed is treated as married. 'Betrothed made equal to married' fits that reading of 'desponsatae adaequatur'.

last_rejected.quote: Elsewhere it may be taken so.
last_rejected.source_quote: Nam alibi ita sane habendum est.
last_rejected.why: The gerundive requires that elsewhere the view must be held, not merely may be.
last_rejected.fix: Elsewhere, indeed, it must be taken so.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Alibi ita sane habendum est' is a concession about other places. 'May be taken so' softens the gerundive, but the concession and its force stay intact.
